description: TLS 1.3 handshake decomposed. The 1-RTT handshake replaced TLS 1.2's 2-RTT design by sending key shares in the first message. Resumption with PSK enables 0-RTT for repeat connections. Forward secrecy is mandatory. The handshake establishes mutual cryptographic context: cipher suite, ephemeral keys, server identity (via certificate), optionally client identity.

sub_mechanisms.name: client_hello_message
sub_mechanisms.definition: First TLS 1.3 message: client sends supported versions, cipher suites, key share (ephemeral public key), and optional extensions (SNI, ALPN, PSK identities).
sub_mechanisms.why: Key share + ciphers + extensions all in the first flight. Server can complete its half of the handshake without an extra round-trip. The fundamental 1-RTT enabler.

sub_mechanisms.name: supported_versions_extension
sub_mechanisms.definition: Lists TLS versions the client supports. TLS 1.3 mandates this extension; legacy version field is set to 1.2 to dodge middleboxes.
sub_mechanisms.why: Middleboxes broke when seeing 'TLS 1.3' in the version field. Extension-based negotiation hides the actual version. Pragmatic concession to protocol ossification.

sub_mechanisms.name: key_share_extension
sub_mechanisms.definition: Client's ephemeral public key for the proposed key-exchange group. Server picks one if matched; otherwise sends HelloRetryRequest specifying a usable group.
sub_mechanisms.why: Eliminates the round-trip TLS 1.2 needed to negotiate the group first then exchange keys. Client speculatively sends a key share for its preferred group; if server can't use it, one extra RTT.

sub_mechanisms.name: server_hello_message
sub_mechanisms.definition: Server's response: selected version, cipher suite, server's key share. Encrypted records begin after this point.
sub_mechanisms.why: Server completes its key exchange + signals the chosen cipher. Everything after this is encrypted using the derived handshake keys. The handshake's privacy point.

sub_mechanisms.name: ECDHE_key_exchange
sub_mechanisms.definition: Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral. Each side has an ephemeral key pair; shared secret is computed via curve point multiplication.
sub_mechanisms.why: Forward secrecy: ephemeral keys are discarded after the session. Future compromise of the server's long-term key doesn't expose past sessions. TLS 1.3 mandates this (no static RSA key exchange).

sub_mechanisms.name: HKDF_key_derivation
sub_mechanisms.definition: HMAC-based Key Derivation Function. Derives multiple keys (handshake encryption, application encryption, exporter) from the master secret + transcript.
sub_mechanisms.why: One shared secret needs to produce multiple uses (client-write, server-write, handshake-traffic, application-traffic). HKDF-Expand-Label gives each use its own derived key with no risk of cross-use.

sub_mechanisms.name: certificate_chain
sub_mechanisms.definition: Server sends its certificate + intermediate CA certificates. Client validates the chain up to a trusted root.
sub_mechanisms.why: Most certificates are issued by intermediate CAs; the trust root is the public root CA. Chain must be complete for client to walk from server cert to root. Missing intermediates is a common deployment issue.

sub_mechanisms.name: certificate_verify_signature
sub_mechanisms.definition: Server signs the handshake transcript with its certificate's private key, proving it holds the key.
sub_mechanisms.why: Authenticates the server's identity. Without this, an attacker with the certificate but not the key could MITM. The signature commits to the entire handshake — attacker can't replay or tamper.

sub_mechanisms.name: finished_message
sub_mechanisms.definition: Each side sends a MAC over the entire handshake transcript using a derived key. Both verify each other's Finished.
sub_mechanisms.why: Closes the loop: each side has proved knowledge of the shared secret + agreement on the handshake bytes. Detection of tampering anywhere in the handshake. Application data may follow.

sub_mechanisms.name: PSK_session_resumption
sub_mechanisms.definition: After a TLS 1.3 handshake, server can send NewSessionTicket messages containing pre-shared keys + lifetimes. Client uses PSK in subsequent handshakes.
sub_mechanisms.why: Avoids the full certificate exchange + signature. PSK-based handshake is 1 RTT or 0 RTT (with early data). Critical for repeat-visit page load times.

sub_mechanisms.name: zero_RTT_early_data
sub_mechanisms.definition: With PSK, client can send application data along with ClientHello. Server can process it before completing the handshake.
sub_mechanisms.why: Eliminates the handshake's last RTT. But replay vulnerable (server can't authenticate the data until handshake completes). Use only for idempotent requests. HTTP GET typically; never for state-changing operations.

sub_mechanisms.name: AEAD_cipher
sub_mechanisms.definition: Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data. AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305. Encrypt + MAC in one operation.
sub_mechanisms.why: TLS 1.3 removed the older MAC-then-Encrypt schemes (BEAST, Lucky 13 vulnerabilities). AEAD is provably secure when used correctly. Single-pass encryption is faster on modern CPUs.

sub_mechanisms.name: ALPN_protocol_negotiation
sub_mechanisms.definition: Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation: client lists protocols (h2, h3, http/1.1); server picks one.
sub_mechanisms.why: Lets HTTP/2 negotiate via TLS without an extra protocol upgrade. Same connection: HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1 by mutual agreement. Required for HTTP/2 over TLS; HTTP/3 uses different mechanism (Alt-Svc).

derivation_rules.name: speculative_key_share_eliminates_rtt
if: client sends key share with first message
then: handshake completes in 1 RTT instead of 2
derivation_rules.why: TLS 1.2 negotiated the group, then exchanged keys — 2 RTTs. TLS 1.3 speculates the group + sends keys; server confirms or requests retry. Most attempts use one of the common groups, so 1 RTT is achieved in practice.

derivation_rules.name: forward_secrecy_protects_past_sessions
if: key exchange uses ephemeral keys discarded after session
then: future key compromise doesn't expose past sessions
derivation_rules.why: ECDHE generates fresh ephemeral keys per handshake; they're never written to disk. Even if the server's long-term private key leaks tomorrow, today's session can't be decrypted. The standard property TLS 1.3 mandates.

derivation_rules.name: AEAD_eliminates_mac_then_encrypt_attacks
if: the cipher provides both confidentiality and authenticity in one operation
derivation_rules.why: Pre-TLS 1.3 used MAC-then-Encrypt; bugs in implementations + protocol design enabled padding oracle attacks. AEAD's atomic construction is provably secure. TLS 1.3 mandates AEAD only.

derivation_rules.name: PSK_resumption_amortises_handshake_cost
if: client and server have a cached PSK
then: future handshakes skip certificate validation + signature
derivation_rules.why: Full handshake includes RSA/ECDSA signature verification (~100k cycles), certificate chain validation. PSK resumption skips these. Repeat-visit page load benefits substantially; major motivation for session caching.

derivation_rules.name: zero_RTT_safe_only_for_idempotent_operations
then: the data may be replayed by an attacker
derivation_rules.why: Server can't distinguish a replayed 0-RTT message from the original until the handshake completes. For idempotent requests (HTTP GET), replay is harmless; for state-changing operations (POST that transfers money), replay is catastrophic. Use 0-RTT carefully.
